Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful
try hard not think about the trauma
I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement

Threat.value: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
I feel like I don't know myself anymore
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette:
Mai, a 37-year-old refugee aid worker, was cycling through a crowded market in a border town when police vehicles surged into the square. She had been delivering food parcels to displaced families; within seconds, officers were swinging batons into the crowd. Her bicycle was knocked over, and she was trampled underfoot, pinned against a stall as people screamed and scattered. She remembers the terror and grief that overwhelmed her—crying for help that never came, feeling the weight of bodies pressing down. In the weeks that followed, she struggled to sleep, waking with her heart pounding, the same terror flooding back. She began to believe that what happened to her was deeply unfair and that nothing was ever done about it. That belief kept the memory alive; she would catch herself revisiting the trampling, searching for a point where someone—anyone—might have helped, as if the injustice had pinned her there in time. That conviction made her feel like she no longer knew herself; she started thinking, “Somebody else would not have let this happen,” though she could not say how they would have escaped. Once she had settled on the idea that she was weak and different, her attention began to snag on things that matched that story—a raised voice, a sudden crowd, the sight of a uniform—each one a potential confirmation of her new view of herself. Because she now saw herself as weak and unable to protect herself, every unexpected sound or dense crowd felt like a genuine danger—she walked into any room already braced, certain that harm could arrive at any moment.

Now, every time Mai sees a police officer, the memory hits her with full force—the grief, the terror, the sense of being overwhelmed. These intrusions come so suddenly that she has to stop whatever she is doing, bracing herself against a wall. Because the memory arrived so vividly and without warning, she started to see its patterns everywhere: a bicycle propped by a lamppost, the sound of a whistle, the particular quality of late-afternoon light that reminded her of the market. She has learned to suppress the thoughts, pushing them down as hard as she can, but this only makes them stronger: a crowded sidewalk will suddenly become that market, and she will be back on the ground. On days when her body felt most on edge—her chest tight, her eyes scanning—the memory would surface as if the threat itself had conjured it, pulling her back into the trampling before she could brace. When the threat felt this close, she had to mentally map every exit in the room and check for obstacles, because planning her escape was the only thing that let her breathe. She also avoids situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful, because hope feels like a trap when injustice is everywhere. Never having let herself stay in a moment long enough to discover it was safe, her nervous system kept the threat level at the same pitch it had been that day, as if the avoidance itself proved the danger was still there. Her husband has noticed she no longer joins him for weekend walks near the park where cyclists pass; seeing people on bicycles triggers the same vivid memories, and she feels a surge of irritability, snapping at him before she can stop herself.

That irritability has bled into her work. As an aid worker, she still goes to crowded distribution sites, but she is increasingly reckless now—taking risks, volunteering for dangerous late-night supply runs because the adrenaline drowns out the memories. Yet those memories always return. When they do, the anger over the injustice resurfaces, and she spirals into gambling. She drives to a small card room two towns over, betting money she cannot afford to lose, distracting herself with the rush of the game. The gambling leaves her hollow, reinforcing her sense of identity loss: she used to be someone who cared, who believed in helping others. Now she feels like a stranger to herself. Her sleep has worsened; she lies awake replaying the event, the terror and grief washing over her until she gives up and scrolls through gambling sites on her phone.

Last month, Mai lost her temper with a volunteer driver after he mentioned that he rides a bicycle to work. She screamed at him, then walked away mid-shift. That outburst frightened her. It also made her realize that the memory is controlling her life—that every time she sees a police car, the injustice flares, and she ends up gambling or snapping. Her husband has said he feels helpless. What finally brought her to a therapist was the fear that she will lose her job and her marriage. She wants to stop the cycle, but she is terrified that facing the memory will break her completely. She hopes, somehow, to find the person she used to be—or at least to sleep through one night without the terror.

violations.explanation: Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that the patient's negative appraisals cause or influence the trauma memory.
Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph shows that negative appraisals lead to the identification or activation of triggers.
Memory → Triggers: No paragraph indicates that the trauma memory causes something to become a trigger; triggers precede memory.
Threat → Memory: No paragraph shows that a sense of threat leads to the trauma memory; threat is a consequence of memory.
Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: No paragraph demonstrates that maladaptive coping strategies result in a sense of threat.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that the patient's negative appraisals cause or influence the trauma memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph shows that negative appraisals lead to the identification or activation of triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: Memory → Triggers: No paragraph indicates that the trauma memory causes something to become a trigger; triggers precede memory.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: Threat → Memory: No paragraph shows that a sense of threat leads to the trauma memory; threat is a consequence of memory.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: No paragraph demonstrates that maladaptive coping strategies result in a sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals (e.g., beliefs about unfairness or weakness) directly cause or increase a sense of threat; the closest references link appraisals to attention or identity, not to perceived danger.

No paragraph conveys that the sense of threat directly drives maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, suppression, gambling); instead, maladaptive strategies are shown as responses to the memory or to negative appraisals, and threat is maintained by avoidance rather than triggered by it.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals (e.g., beliefs about unfairness or weakness) directly cause or increase a sense of threat; the closest references link appraisals to attention or identity, not to perceived danger.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."
  e.g. "The belief that she was a target — not unlucky, but chosen — meant that every unfamiliar face carried a weight of potential danger."
  e.g. "Her certainty that she couldn't protect herself made every new situation feel like a test she was already failing."
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: No paragraph conveys that the sense of threat directly drives maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, suppression, gambling); instead, maladaptive strategies are shown as responses to the memory or to negative appraisals, and threat is maintained by avoidance rather than triggered by it.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
